task_description:
You are a trail condition tagging service. You receive one free-text field report about a section of trail and you return the condition tags that apply, as JSON. Output only the JSON object: no prose, no explanation, no markdown code fences.

The output object has exactly one key: {"tags": [<tag code>, ...]}. The list may be empty. List tags in the order the taxonomy below gives them.

THE TAXONOMY. These are the only tag codes that exist. Use them verbatim; never invent a code, never paraphrase one, and never emit a code that is not listed here.

IMPASSABLE:
  BRIDGE_OUT: a built crossing is destroyed, missing, or unusable
  FORD_UNSAFE: an unbridged crossing cannot be crossed safely at present
  WASHOUT_MAJOR: the tread is gone to a landslide or flood scar and there is no safe way across the scar
  BURN_CLOSURE: the trail lies inside a posted or active burn closure

OBSTRUCTION:
  BLOWDOWN_HEAVY: downed trees must be climbed over or bushwhacked around (as opposed to stepped over)
  BLOWDOWN_LIGHT: downed trees can be stepped over without leaving the tread (as opposed to climbed over)
  DRAIN_BLOCKED: a drainage structure such as a water bar or culvert is clogged; use this for a failed structure, not for water on the tread with no structure at fault
  SIGN_DAMAGED: signage is broken, illegible, or points the wrong way

SEASONAL:
  SNOW_PATCH: lingering snow that can be crossed or walked around (as opposed to continuous cover)
  SNOW_CONTINUOUS: snow covers the route continuously and route-finding is needed (as opposed to isolated patches)
  WATER_LOW: seasonal water sources are dry or nearly dry; this is about sources, never about how far apart they are
  RUNOFF_ON_TREAD: melt or rainwater runs down the trail itself with no drainage structure at fault; a clogged structure is DRAIN_BLOCKED instead

COMFORT:
  BUG_PRESSURE: mosquitoes or flies are bad enough to affect the trip
  WATER_CARRY_LONG: the distance between available water sources requires carrying; this is about how far apart sources are, not about sources being dry
  CAMP_SITES_FULL: established campsites are all occupied
  PARKING_FULL: trailhead parking is at capacity

RULE 1 - Apply a tag only when the report describes the condition that tag's definition names. Several tags are close neighbours and are told apart only by their definitions above, so read them rather than matching on surface words: WATER_LOW is about sources being dry while WATER_CARRY_LONG is about how far apart sources are; RUNOFF_ON_TREAD is water on the trail with no structure at fault while DRAIN_BLOCKED is a failed structure; BLOWDOWN_HEAVY is climbed over while BLOWDOWN_LIGHT is stepped over; SNOW_PATCH can be walked around while SNOW_CONTINUOUS needs route-finding.

RULE 2 - The override. If ANY tag from the IMPASSABLE family applies, the answer contains ONLY the IMPASSABLE tags. Every OBSTRUCTION, SEASONAL and COMFORT tag is dropped, even when the report describes those conditions clearly and at length. A blocked trail is reported as blocked and nothing else.

RULE 3 - If no tag applies, return an empty list. A report of a trail in good condition is {"tags": []}. Never reach for the closest tag to avoid returning nothing.

RULE 4 - Every report carries a date and a mileage figure. Neither ever affects the tags. Ignore them.

Every report is a first-person trip report. It opens with the date and the mileage, then describes the section in plain sentences. No other format ever appears.

Example.
Input: Trip report, 2026-July 19. We covered 8.4 miles out and back. Mosquitoes were brutal the entire way. The footbridge at the lower crossing is gone entirely. The trailhead lot was full early.
Output: {"tags": ["BRIDGE_OUT"]}
(BRIDGE_OUT is IMPASSABLE, so Rule 2 fires: BUG_PRESSURE and PARKING_FULL are dropped even though the report states both.)
synthetic_data_generation_instructions:
Each input is one free-text trail condition field report, and nothing else. Every report is a first-person trip report of several sentences, and no other register ever appears. It opens with the line 'Trip report, <date>. We covered <n> miles out and back.' and continues with plain sentences about the section. Never write a logbook entry, a ranger patrol note, a crew work report or a satellite message. The date and the mileage figure are decorative: vary them freely and never let them affect the tags.

A report describes between zero and four taggable conditions, and always also contains one to three sentences of incidental detail that maps to no tag at all -- wildlife, views, flowers, light, timing, camp chat. Describe conditions in the reporter's own natural words rather than restating a tag's definition, and never name a tag code inside the report text.

Across the dataset, cover the whole taxonomy: every family appears often, and the close-neighbour tags appear as distinct cases so the discriminator matters (sources dry versus sources far apart, water on tread versus a clogged structure, blowdown climbed over versus stepped over, snow patches versus continuous snow). A substantial share of reports describe an IMPASSABLE condition alongside several other conditions, so the override rule is exercised, and a substantial share describe a trail in good order so the answer is an empty tag list.

Apply the override on every row before writing its tags: when any IMPASSABLE tag applies, the answer holds only the IMPASSABLE tags, and every other condition in the report is dropped. Use only tag codes from the taxonomy, spelled exactly as listed.
llm_as_a_judge_instructions: The prediction is good (1) only if it is a single valid JSON object with one key "tags" whose value is a list of tag codes, and nothing else: no prose, no explanation, no markdown code fences. Every code must be a code from the taxonomy in the task description, written verbatim. Then check the tags against the field report and the rules in the task description: every condition the report describes must have its tag unless the IMPASSABLE override drops it, no tag may be present for a condition the report does not describe, the IMPASSABLE override must be applied when it fires, and an empty list is good only if the report describes nothing reportable. Ignore the order of the tags and whitespace. Mark the prediction bad (0) if any of these checks fails.
trace_processing_instructions:
These are field reports logged by a legacy tagging service whose answers are often wrong. Rewrite the answer to the correct tag set for the report as written, applying the override and empty-list rules strictly. Never edit the report text itself: the reporter's wording, date and mileage stay exactly as they are.

The assistant message content is itself a JSON object and must be emitted as a compact single-line JSON string of exactly the form {"tags": [...]}, with no surrounding prose, no markdown code fence, and no trailing commentary. When that object is carried inside a larger JSON structure, escape its quotes correctly so the outer structure stays valid JSON. Emit no reasoning or explanation anywhere in the rewritten conversation. The content must never be empty: a report with no applicable tags is the non-empty string {"tags": []}.

Check the override before writing the answer. Work out every tag the report supports, then ask whether any of them is in the IMPASSABLE family; if one is, delete every OBSTRUCTION, SEASONAL and COMFORT tag from the answer and keep only the IMPASSABLE ones. Legacy answers frequently get this wrong by keeping the other conditions, and copying that mistake is the single most damaging error you can make here.
